strengths: Novel application of conformal prediction to learn early stopping criteria for exact MIP solving, with rigorous distribution-free probabilistic guarantees on solution quality
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 correctly establishes conformal calibration via exchangeability, and Theorems 5.1-5.2 provide sample-conditional concentration bounds
Substantial practical speedups: 60-95% solve time reduction on most problem families while maintaining ≥95% success rate at 0.1%-optimality
Well-motivated formulation clearly illustrated in Figure 1; the three-step pipeline (train, calibrate, deploy) is clean and practical
Comprehensive experiments across 6 diverse problem families and 2 solvers with detailed results and honest limitations discussion
Technically sound: the squashing function ensures valid predictions, weighted loss focuses on critical regions, and mathematical framework is rigorous
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (conformal prediction, neural network predictors) in straightforward manner; Theorems 5.1-5.2 apply standard concentration bounds
Problem-dependent effectiveness severely limits impact: GISP achieves only 8% speedup; paper lacks characterization of which problem structures benefit from early stopping or why
Predictor quality dependence not characterized: no analysis of prediction error rates, failure modes, or conditions for good performance; no comparison to simpler baselines
Insufficient ablation studies: missing sensitivity analyses for network architecture, calibration set size, weighting function, and discretization step; no per-instance analysis
Strong unexamined assumptions: equation 3.2 assumes theta and t uniquely identify algorithm state only on same hardware; weighting function (Eq. 5) with 1/y_theta(t) may cause numerical instability
Unexplained experimental results: OTS-medium shows CP_COPT with 78.6% success rate despite conformal calibration guaranteeing ~95%; discrepancy needs explanation
Limited distribution shift investigation: acknowledges distribution shift sensitivity but provides no empirical analysis of robustness to domain shift
Expensive training requirement: requires solving instances to completion, limiting applicability to problems already solvable; does not extend frontier of tractable instances
Missing critical analyses: no failure mode characterization, limited investigation of generalization across problem families, no computational cost analysis of predictor inference

strengths: Sound theoretical framework with rigorous conformal prediction calibration and sample-conditional concentration guarantees
Addresses a practical problem: MIP solvers often find optimal solutions long before proving optimality
Achieves substantial speedups (60-95%) on several problem families while maintaining near-optimal solution quality
Well-written with clear problem formulation and detailed experimental setup
Honest discussion of limitations including expensive training requirements and distribution shift assumptions
weaknesses: Critical empirical inconsistency: MVC results show 88% of instances are ε-optimal, notably below the claimed 95% guarantee. This discrepancy is not adequately explained and raises serious questions about methodology or guarantee validity

Limited technical novelty: straightforward combination of established conformal prediction with LSTM-based gap prediction. Theorems 4.1-5.2 apply standard results without significant innovation. Distinction from Clarke & Stellato (2025) is unclear

Narrow experimental validation: only 6 problem families from one benchmark; no cross-family generalization experiments; no out-of-distribution robustness testing; no ablation studies; missing comparisons to other learning-based acceleration methods

Method fundamentally limited to problem instances with large gaps between finding and proving optimality, as evidenced by GISP showing only 8% speedup. This key limitation is not upfront characterized or predictable

Critical gap between theory and practice: Guarantees hold for any predictor, but meaningful speedup requires accuracy. Section 5.3 acknowledges this but provides no analysis of predictor quality, calibration failures, or robustness to early pessimistic predictions

Expensive practical requirements: requires solving all training instances (preprocessing cost), only accelerates already-solvable problems, assumes test distribution matches training distribution perfectly

Insufficient investigation of design choices: loss weighting (Eq. 5) could be unstable when yθ(t) is very small; rolling minimum design choice ḡθ(t) not justified; rolling minimum locks threshold after first low prediction
Missing statistical rigor: no significance testing; no investigation of why correctness varies from 88% to 98% across families; unexplained variation undermines confidence in method reliability

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Rather than accelerating solvers internally, the paper learns when to terminate early—a fundamentally different and creative approach that is well-motivated by Figure 1
Rigorous theoretical guarantees: Theorems 4.1, 5.1, and 5.2 provide distribution-free and sample-conditional coverage guarantees with sound proofs based on conformal prediction and VC-dimension
Strong experimental results: Achieves 60-95% speedups on most benchmark families while maintaining 0.1%-optimality with 95% probability, tested on two solvers (Gurobi, COPT) and real-world instances
Practical applicability: Method only requires solver state features (bounds, time, nodes), not full problem formulation, making it straightforward to implement
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with good motivation, clear problem formulation (Section 3), and detailed experimental setup with promised code availability
Honest limitations discussion: Paper explicitly identifies distribution shift assumption, problem-dependent speedups, and computational training costs
weaknesses: Computational training cost not fully characterized: While acknowledged as 'computationally intensive,' the overhead of solving 800 instances per problem family is never quantified. No amortized cost analysis or break-even point is provided, which is critical for practitioners

Missing predictor quality analysis: No prediction accuracy metrics (MAE, RMSE) reported. Section 5.3 acknowledges that poor predictions yield no speedup, but no empirical evidence of predictor quality across problem families is provided

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Only simple heuristics compared (terminate after N solutions). No comparison to other learned early stopping methods or to Clarke & Stellato (2025) which uses conformal prediction on MIPs

Missing critical ablation studies: No sensitivity analysis for calibration set size (ranges from c=28 to c=100), LSTM architecture not justified, weighting scheme w(t)∝1/y(t) presented without empirical validation of alternatives

Problem-dependent effectiveness limits scope: GISP achieves only 8% speedup, and no analysis explains which problem characteristics lead to large vs. small speedups. Method cannot extend to previously unsolvable instances

Weak statistical rigor: Figure 3 shows error bars but no significance tests. Unclear if results are averaged over multiple random seeds. Some improvements appear modest but statistical significance is not established

Distribution shift assumption unstated: The critical assumption that test instances are drawn from the training/calibration distribution is not emphasized in main text and no robustness analysis is provided
Calibration set size variation unexplained: Different problems use c∈{28,100}. Impact on coverage guarantees not discussed (OTS-medium with c=28 has weaker guarantees)

strengths: Technically sound theoretical contributions: Theorems 4.1-5.3 rigorously establish probabilistic guarantees using conformal prediction, with clever handling of continuous time trajectories via rolling minimums and left-inverses
Novel application: First to apply conformal prediction for accelerating exact MIP solving while providing formal guarantees; distinct conceptual approach (early stopping vs. improving proof search)
Significant practical speedups: 60-95% solve time reduction on 5/6 benchmark families while maintaining 0.1%-optimality with 95% probability
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Six diverse problem families, two solvers, extensive appendices with sensitivity analyses, convergence curves, and ablation studies
Correctly handles multiple testing: The remark in Section 4.1 identifies and properly addresses the multiple testing problem through pre-calibrated thresholds
Well-presented paper: Clear motivation, logical development from problem to theory to experiments, honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Severe practical limitations on applicability: Requires solving hundreds of instances to completion beforehand to obtain optimal values and solver trajectories. This is computationally expensive and infeasible when optimal solutions are unknown a priori, limiting real-world deployment

Critical gap between theory and practice: No analysis of how predictor quality affects theoretical guarantees. Section 5.4 admits poor predictors yield no speedup, but robustness of conformal guarantees to predictor errors is not characterized

Incomplete cost accounting: Training time (~30 min/GPU), calibration overhead (100 instances), and callback evaluation costs not amortized into speedup metrics. Fair comparison should include total end-to-end cost
Inconsistent performance across problem families: GISP achieves only 8% speedup vs. 60-95% on others. Root cause and conditions for method applicability not thoroughly explained

Unhandled edge cases: Paper does not address solver behavior when hitting time/memory limits before convergence (violating Assumption 3.1), infeasible/unbounded instances, or robustness to solver configuration changes
Distribution-specific training: Method requires separate training/calibration for each problem family. Cannot transfer knowledge across problem classes, severely limiting scope and practical impact

strengths: Clear problem motivation with effective illustration of the optimality-gap inefficiency
Rigorous conformal prediction framework with distribution-free guarantees (Theorem 4.1) and sample-conditional bounds (Theorems 5.1-5.3)
Elegant handling of multiple-testing problem through pre-calibrated threshold
Strong empirical results on tested domains: 60%+ speedups on most Distributional MIPLIB families while maintaining ~95% coverage
Comprehensive experimental presentation with detailed appendices, sensitivity analyses, and convergence visualizations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies standard conformal prediction methods (Angelopoulos & Bates 2021) with straightforward LSTM prediction, requiring no algorithmic innovation
Narrow experimental scope: all experiments on Distributional MIPLIB procedurally-generated problems; only 2 real-world instances; unclear generalization to diverse MIP types
Strong distributional assumption: requires test instances from same distribution as calibration data; Theorem 5.3 on distribution shift lacks empirical validation
Substantial computational overhead not analyzed: 30-min GPU training + 800 complete solves per problem family, but no cost-benefit analysis of when this investment pays off

Insufficient predictor analysis: no ablation studies on LSTM architecture; appendices show simpler models (linear, UB-rate heuristic) match LSTM performance; Section 5.4 admits guarantees hold for any predictor
Unexplained problem-dependent performance: GISP achieves only 8% speedup vs. 60%+ elsewhere; no analysis of what problem properties enable/disable early stopping
Weak baseline comparisons: only compares to standard solver termination (not a learned method); missing comparisons to learned branching policies and other ML acceleration techniques
Coverage gaps: Figure 4 shows variable coverage (85-97%) across problems; Table 16 shows coverage drops to 75-80% with small calibration sets; limited guidance on choosing calibration set size
No cross-domain or few-shot learning evaluation: same LSTM architecture used across all families; no evidence of generalization across problem types
Incomplete methodology: sensitivity to time-weighting function unexplored; behavior when z*(θ)≈0 unclear; squashing function (Eq. 3) not justified

strengths: Novel application of conformal prediction to accelerate exact MIP solving with rigorous probabilistic guarantees; first work of this kind
Solid theoretical framework with three complementary theorems (4.1, 5.1-5.3) providing distribution-free and sample-conditional guarantees
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on six diverse problem families including real-world datasets, with thorough ablation studies and sensitivity analyses
Significant practical speedups (60-95% on most benchmarks) while maintaining solution quality guarantees
Elegant technical approach using squashing function to constrain predictions and weighted loss to focus on decision region
Honest and complete presentation with clear limitations section and supplementary materials
Multiple-testing insight—conformal prediction avoids hypothesis-testing inflation from solver callbacks
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily combines LSTM and conformal prediction without introducing new techniques
Scope limited to accelerating solvable problems; does not extend tractable frontier or improve solver fundamentals
Significant problem-dependent performance variation (8% speedup on GISP vs. 60-95% on others) with limited analysis of when method succeeds
Requires expensive upfront collection of training data from target distribution; only works reliably in-distribution
Incomplete analysis of predictor quality's impact on speedup; heuristic baselines in appendix are simplistic
Artificial experimental setup—presolve disabled, single-threaded execution, specific MIPFocus settings
Calibration set size guidance lacking; high coverage variance with small calibration sets; OTS-medium compromises on c=28
Limited comparison to other learning-to-optimize methods; no empirical comparison to Clarke & Stellato (2025) despite mentioning it
Multiple-testing argument in Section 4.1 could provide stronger justification for rolling minimum approach
Presentation issues: notation sometimes introduced before explanation, technical definitions lack intuition, key details relegated to appendix
